sections.purpose: To measure arterial blood pressure in human subjects accurately using a manual aneroid or mercury sphygmomanometer as part of clinical pharmacology practicals.
sections.scope: Applicable to clinical pharmacology practicals in the Pharmacology department for measuring systolic and diastolic blood pressure.
procedure: Ensure the subject has been seated quietly for at least 5 minutes before measurement.
Instruct the subject to avoid caffeine, exercise, and smoking for 30 minutes prior to measurement.
Seat the subject comfortably with back supported, feet flat on the floor, and arm at heart level.
Select the appropriate cuff size: the bladder should encircle at least 80% of the upper arm.
Wrap the cuff snugly around the bare upper arm, 2–3 cm above the antecubital fossa.
Palpate the brachial artery and place the stethoscope diaphragm over it.
Close the air release valve on the bulb and inflate the cuff to 30 mmHg above the expected systolic pressure (or until radial pulse disappears).
Slowly deflate the cuff at a rate of 2–3 mmHg per second by gently opening the release valve.
Note the pressure at which the first Korotkoff sound (faint tapping) is heard — this is the systolic pressure.
Continue deflating and note the pressure at which sounds disappear completely — this is the diastolic pressure (Korotkoff phase V).
Fully deflate the cuff and remove it from the arm.
Record both systolic and diastolic values in mmHg along with the arm used and patient position.
Repeat measurement after 1–2 minutes and take the average if required.
Document findings in the practical record with date, time, and subject details.
precautions: Use a calibrated and validated sphygmomanometer for accurate readings.
Ensure proper cuff size selection — too small a cuff gives falsely high readings.
The cuff should not be applied over clothing.
Do not deflate the cuff too rapidly — maintain 2–3 mmHg/second deflation rate.
Avoid taking measurements immediately after physical exertion.
Inspect the equipment for leaks, cracked tubing, or defective valves before use.
Mercury sphygmomanometers must be handled with care — spillage must be managed per hazardous material protocol.
Calibrate the device at regular intervals as per manufacturer's instructions.
